title: Graph-R1: Towards Agentic GraphRAG Framework via End-to-end Reinforcement Learning
one_liner: Turn graph-based retrieval into a multi-turn search policy that can ask for more graph evidence step by step, so grounded answering improves without one oversized retrieval pass.
lead: Standard retrieval-augmented generation often pulls a handful of text chunks once and hopes that the answer is already present. Graph-based retrieval improves this by connecting entities and relations, but many graph systems still retrieve only once, then dump a large context into the answer model. Graph-R1 changes the problem into an interactive search process. It builds a lightweight knowledge hypergraph, lets a policy decide which graph region to inspect next, and trains the full retrieval process end to end with reinforcement learning. The system can therefore refine its search over several turns instead of committing all retrieval choices in one pass.

paras: In one-shot retrieval, the system chooses context before it has seen how the reasoning will unfold. If the first retrieval misses one important entity or relation, the answer stage has no good way to recover. It is forced to reason with incomplete evidence.

Graph retrieval helps because a graph makes entity and relation structure explicit. But if the graph is still queried only once, the system keeps the same weakness: it cannot ask a follow-up graph question after seeing partial evidence. That limitation matters on multi-hop tasks where the answer appears only after traversing several linked facts.

callout.html: Treat retrieval as a step-by-step decision process over a graph, because later search choices should depend on what earlier graph evidence has already revealed.

steps.text: Represent entities and linked facts in a graph structure that keeps relation information without the full cost of a heavy graph build.
Map the user question to relevant starting points in the graph so retrieval begins near likely evidence.

steps.b: Take one graph action at a time.
steps.text: At each turn, choose whether to inspect another node, follow a relation, or stop because the answer evidence is already sufficient.
Train the policy end to end so graph actions that lead to accurate, efficient answers receive higher reward.
Use the gathered graph path and attached facts to generate the final response with better grounding because the answer can point back to the exact entities and relations that were retrieved.

paras: The paper changes graph retrieval from one fixed pre-answer lookup into a multi-turn search policy over graph actions.
object.object: the retrieval policy over graph evidence

hidden.name: marginal retrieval value of the next graph step
paras: The hidden quantity is whether one more graph action will add enough new evidence to justify its cost. The system should continue searching when the current evidence is incomplete and stop when the answer is already well supported.

That quantity is difficult to estimate with fixed retrieval because the model never observes an intermediate state. Graph-R1 makes it observable by turning retrieval into a sequence. After each turn, the policy can ask whether the newest node or relation reduced uncertainty enough to change the answer.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark retrieval states where another graph step is still worth taking because it adds new supporting evidence.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether the next graph hop will still teach the system something needed for the answer.

The method optimizes graph retrieval as an agent-environment interaction, so the policy can learn when additional graph exploration improves grounded generation by adding missing support and when it should stop because the current path already supports the answer.

paras: Many questions are multi-hop. You might first find the right entity, then follow a relation to another entity, then verify one attached fact before answering. A one-shot retriever has to guess that whole chain in advance. If any link is missed, the answer stage receives broken evidence.

Graph-R1 avoids that brittleness by making retrieval sequential. Each graph step is chosen after seeing the evidence from the previous one. That allows the policy to redirect the search when one branch looks weak because the newly retrieved facts do not support the query, and to continue along a promising branch when support is accumulating because each new node reinforces the same answer path.

Reinforcement learning is useful here because the quality of one graph step is defined by what it enables later. A step that looks small locally can still be decisive if it opens the branch that contains the needed fact. End-to-end reward can capture that delayed value better than a one-step heuristic can because the final return credits early steps that make later successful retrieval possible.

stages.s: choose next graph action from partial evidence

math.h2: Choose retrieval paths with cumulative reward
math.words: A concise summary is to score a retrieval path by answer quality minus the cost of the graph actions needed to build that path.
symbols: the sequence of graph actions taken before answering
how accurate and grounded the final answer is after following that path
the total cost of graph search steps along that path

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Path A stops after one node and yields answer quality 6 with cost 1.
Path B follows two extra relations and yields answer quality 10 with cost 3.
Path B wins because the extra graph search adds enough grounded evidence to justify its cost.

math.note: The real training objective is a reinforcement-learning return, but this simplified score captures the paper's point: keep only graph exploration that pays for itself in answer quality.

charts.title: One-shot retrieval baselines
charts.note: Fixed retrieval often misses later hops because it must commit before seeing intermediate graph evidence.

charts.title: Graph-R1
charts.note: The paper reports gains on standard retrieval benchmarks because the policy can spend extra graph steps only where those steps improve grounded answering.

items.b: The lightweight graph can drop key structure.
items.html: If graph construction omits a needed relation, then no retrieval policy can recover it because the evidence path does not exist in the graph.
Without strong penalties or stop control, the policy may revisit the same nodes because sequential retrieval creates more opportunities for wasted motion.

items.b: Reward can overfit one benchmark style.
items.html: A policy tuned on one family of graph questions may learn shallow traversal habits that do not transfer because the delayed reward pattern changes on other datasets.

The method works when the graph is informative and the reward balances quality with retrieval cost, because the policy can then continue graph search only where another step adds real grounding value.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small knowledge graph question-answering setup with multi-hop questions. Compare three systems: one-shot text retrieval, one-shot graph retrieval, and interactive graph retrieval with a learned stop decision. Log the sequence of visited nodes and relations so you can inspect whether later graph actions added new supporting evidence.

The demo should show that the interactive graph retriever takes extra steps mainly on questions that truly require them and stops early on simple questions, because retrieval is being controlled by cumulative answer value rather than by a fixed one-pass budget.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show that multi-turn graph retrieval improves grounded answers by adapting the search path after each retrieved fact, because that is the core difference from one-shot GraphRAG.
